title: Students in the room
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in paediatrics. You need to examine Jacob, 14, who has had a dull ache and a soft swelling in his scrotum for three weeks. He is otherwise well. Three medical students are with you, and his mother is present.

Jacob looks very embarrassed.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Tell him the students need to learn.
options.detailed: Students do need to learn, but not at the cost of his dignity.

options.text: Ask his mother whether she minds the medical students staying for the examination.
options.detailed: At 14, he can decide about this.

options.text: Ask Jacob privately whether the students can stay.
options.brief: He should decide who is present.
options.detailed: Patients should be asked before students are present, especially for intimate examinations. Asking him privately makes it easier to say no.

options.text: Ask the students to wait outside if he prefers.
options.detailed: The students can learn another time.

options.text: Examine him quickly to minimise embarrassment.
Keep him covered, and explain what you'll do.
options.detailed: Explaining and minimising exposure reduces embarrassment.

options.text: Ask one student to stay as a chaperone.
options.brief: A student isn't a suitable chaperone.
options.detailed: A chaperone should be a trained staff member.
He should decide who is present.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you protect a young person's dignity and ask for his consent before an intimate examination with students present.
explanation.keyDetails: He is 14 and embarrassed. Students are present. The examination is intimate.
explanation.reasoning: [C] asks him, [D] respects his choice, and [F] protects his dignity. The distractors pressure him ([A]), bypass him ([B], [H]), or fail to address consent ([E], [G]).
explanation.competing: [B] may seem respectful, but he should be asked himself.
